Thank you for joining us. This paper asks why citizens who live under the same democratic institutions differ in their support for the rules that keep those institutions democratic. We bring together three bodies of work that are often discussed separately: cultural orientations towards hierarchy and social harmony, political efficacy, and the relationship between trust in government and perceived government performance. Australia is the case. I will start with the outcome we want to explain, then introduce the two cultural orientations and the political judgements in our account. After describing the survey, I will focus on the findings that most clearly distinguish the proposed relationships.

Our starting point is a familiar ambiguity in survey research. A respondent may say that democracy is desirable and still think a government should be able to silence hostile news coverage or ignore a court decision. The disagreement is about the rules that allow citizens to contest power while a government is in office, as well as the rules for replacing it at an election. So our question is about commitment to those specific principles. We want to know whether beliefs about authority and disagreement help explain that commitment, and whether citizens' views of their own political capacity and of government performance add to the explanation. - Lower absolute bar, not the

This is why the measure developed by Claassen and colleagues is useful for our purposes. It asks about concrete permissions a government might claim, rather than relying on a general declaration of support for democracy. The seven items cover electoral competition and equal voting rights, along with media freedom and constraints on executive power. We code responses so that rejecting a government's permission to breach these principles means stronger support for liberal democracy. The items are treated as ordered indicators of one underlying support factor. We are therefore studying support for liberal democracy in a specific institutional sense, not satisfaction with the current government.

Our cultural argument separates two orientations that can be lost when studies speak of Asian values as one disposition. Vertical orientation is about deference within unequal relationships. The questions ask whether people should comply with unreasonable demands from parents and whether teachers' authority should be questioned. Harmony orientation concerns the social costs of division and divergent ways of thinking. Both might matter for democratic contestation, but for different reasons: one concerns the standing of authority, and the other concerns open disagreement. These items were adapted from the Asian Barometer Survey. We use them with Australian respondents to examine particular beliefs, without assigning a regional or ethnic identity to anyone who endorses them.

We then consider two kinds of political judgement. Internal efficacy asks whether I think I can understand and discuss politics. External efficacy asks whether I think politicians listen to people like me. Those beliefs can diverge: someone may feel capable of making a judgement while doubting that office-holders will respond. The second judgement concerns trust. Norris asks us to consider whether confidence in an agent fits the agent's performance. Our survey cannot audit performance, but it can tell us whether a person's trust in the federal government sits alongside a perception that a serious problem exists. This lets us study the terms on which confidence is maintained. “ochlocracy” 暴民政治

Here is the four-part classification. A respondent who trusts the federal government and does not see the specified problem as severe is classified as sceptically trusting. A respondent who withholds trust and sees a severe problem is classified as sceptically mistrustful. The two mismatches are cynical mistrust, meaning non-trust without a severe problem assessment, and credulous trust, meaning trust despite one. We construct the classification twice: once with perceived corruption and once with perceived problems in critical service delivery. These are descriptions of paired survey responses. In particular, non-trust includes the midpoint, and the problem questions concern Australia broadly rather than independently verified federal-government performance.

This figure places the outcome on the right. On the left are the two cultural orientations; in the middle are internal and external efficacy and the four trust relationships. We expect cultural orientations to have their own associations with support. They may also be associated with how citizens assess their political capacity, government responsiveness, and the fit between trust and perceived performance. Efficacy can enter the trust classification as well as the support equation. The arrows organise the theoretical argument, but the empirical blocks are fitted separately. I will return to that distinction when showing the results: this diagram is not evidence that a causal chain or an indirect effect has been established.

The first two expectations concern the direct cultural associations with democratic support. We then separate the proposed efficacy relationships. For harmony, we expect concern about disagreement to accompany lower confidence in one's own political ability; greater internal efficacy should, in turn, accompany stronger support. For vertical orientation, we expect deference to accompany a stronger belief that authorities listen and respond. We also expect that belief, external efficacy, to be associated with weaker support after the other model terms are considered.

Norris's account gives us two distinct expectations about apparent mismatches between trust and perceived performance. We expect lower democratic support among those who continue to trust despite seeing a severe problem, and among those who withhold trust without seeing such a problem. These are separate tests: the two types need not have the same association. Finally, we expect vertical orientation to make credulous trust more likely relative to sceptical trust. Here we compare categories, rather than treating trust relationships as points on an ordered scale.

Australia is useful here because the question is not confined to a democracy in acute crisis. Liberal institutions are established and voting is compulsory, so electoral politics is part of ordinary civic life. We can ask whether support for the principles behind those institutions still varies, and whether our proposed orientations help explain that variation. The case also takes measures associated with the Asian-values debate into an Australian setting. For the trust analysis, the federal government provides one common national object. The performance questions ask about corruption and critical services across Australia, however, and responsibilities for those matters can sit at different levels of government. That difference is important when we interpret the trust categories.

The data come from a national online survey fielded in July 2026. Of the respondents allocated to this research, 1,509 received the seven support items. We first estimate associations between the cultural orientations and the two efficacy measures. We then classify trust relationships and compare the other three types with sceptical trust in multinomial models. Finally, separate latent-support models use corruption and service delivery as the respective criteria for the trust classification. Survey weights are applied throughout, and each equation adjusts for age, political interest, gender and education. The central support analyses include just over 1,200 respondents. Because this is an online panel, the weights do not remove every possible source of selection.

These are the first four items in the concise battery developed by Claassen and colleagues. The slide uses the short item labels from their paper and the wording fielded in our Australian survey. Respondents indicate agreement or disagreement with each statement. Disagreement signals stronger support for the relevant democratic principle.

These three items concern constraints on governing authority. Along with the four items on the previous slide, they form the seven ordered indicators in the latent support model. The battery does not include Claassen and colleagues' separate component on whether key decision-makers are elected. Among respondents who answered all seven items, both the raw and ordinal reliability estimates are high.

These categories are not rare edge cases. With corruption as the criterion, sceptical mistrust accounts for 39 per cent of valid responses and credulous trust for about 12 per cent. With critical service delivery, the corresponding shares are 34 and 12 per cent. So roughly one respondent in eight trusts the federal government while also describing the relevant problem as severe. The classifications overlap, but they are not interchangeable: among respondents who can be classified both ways, just over 70 per cent receive the same type. That gives us a reason to keep both performance criteria in view rather than treating one as a substitute for the other.

Before turning to the associations, we checked how the principal measures work in this survey. The seven items on electoral and liberal-democratic principles have high internal consistency among the 1,288 respondents who answered every item. We treat their ordered responses as indicators of one support factor. The two efficacy pairs also hold together well. The cultural pairs are less closely related to one another, especially the two harmony items. That does not make them unusable, but it matters for interpretation: they capture particular beliefs about deference and disagreement, rather than every aspect of hierarchy or social harmony. The appendix gives the full item wording, coding and response coverage.

We begin with the direct cultural associations. A one-standard-deviation increase in vertical orientation is associated with a reduction of about one quarter of a unit on the latent support scale. The estimate is nearly the same whether the trust relationship is defined with corruption or service delivery. Harmony orientation has a similarly consistent negative association, a little above two tenths of a unit in both models. These estimates are conditional on efficacy, trust type and the controls. They support the two parts of H1, and they tell us that the measured orientations retain an association with liberal-democratic support that is not exhausted by the political judgements included here.

The efficacy results are less symmetrical. Vertical orientation is positively associated with external efficacy: respondents who endorse more deference are also more likely to believe politicians listen and respond. In both support models, external efficacy is then associated with weaker support for liberal democracy, conditional on the other terms. That may seem surprising if responsiveness is assumed to be uniformly beneficial. One possibility is that people who expect authorities to listen see less immediate reason to insist on limits to their power. The harmony-to-internal-efficacy estimate points in the predicted negative direction but is uncertain. Internal efficacy has a small positive association with support only in the corruption model. So the proposed harmony route receives much less consistent evidence than the vertical and external-efficacy pattern.

Turning to the trust relationships, sceptical trust is the comparison category. The largest contrast is credulous trust: people who trust the federal government despite reporting a severe problem express weaker support for liberal-democratic principles under both criteria. The association is larger when the perceived problem is corruption, although these two coefficients have not been formally compared. Cynical mistrust does not show the reduction we predicted, and neither does sceptical mistrust in the central models. This is why we retain four categories rather than simply separating trust from mistrust or combining both apparent mismatches. The result is about citizens' expressed support for democratic rules; it does not tell us whether any individual has assessed government performance correctly.

We also ask whether vertical orientation is associated with the kind of trust a person expresses. Relative to sceptical trust, a one-standard-deviation increase in vertical orientation corresponds to a relative-risk ratio of 1.47 for credulous trust when service delivery is the performance criterion. The corruption estimate points in the same direction, at 1.24, but its p-value is just above .05. The more convincing evidence for H5 therefore comes from the service-delivery classification. These ratios describe comparisons between nominal categories. They should not be read as movement up or down a single ordered trust scale.

This figure brings the supported paths together. The two panels use the same trust object, the federal government, while changing the perceived problem used to classify the trust relationship. Dashed paths show the direct negative associations of vertical and harmony orientations with support. In both panels, vertical orientation is positively associated with external efficacy, while external efficacy and credulous trust are negatively associated with support. The service-delivery panel also shows the vertical-to-credulous contrast. In the corruption panel, internal efficacy is positively associated with support and with the relative likelihood of credulous trust. The labels use B for unstandardised coefficients and RRR for relative-risk ratios. These are associations assembled from compatible but separately fitted equations; the drawing does not establish an indirect effect.

We checked how much depends on the measurement choices. Adding a third harmony item leaves the central credulous-trust contrasts close to their original estimates. Changing the trust object to courts has a larger consequence: all three non-reference types then show lower support than sceptical trust. Changing the threshold to explicit distrust also matters. The federal-government credulous contrast remains negative under corruption, while under service delivery it is no longer clearly detected. Finally, when we pool credulous trust and cynical mistrust into one binary mismatch category, the pooled association is negative. That result conceals the difference between the two types. The main claim is therefore specific to the federal-government classification and is better described with four relationship types.

What do these findings add to the argument? First, the two groups with the clearest trust contrast both report confidence in the federal government. What separates them is their assessment of a serious problem. That is the part a simple trust score would miss. Second, the absence of a negative association for cynical or sceptical mistrust cautions against treating mistrust of a government as opposition to democratic rules. Norris's work on critical citizens suggests one reason people may withhold confidence while valuing the liberties and constraints that let them hold authorities to account. We do not observe that motive directly. Finally, the two cultural orientations retain negative associations with support after the political judgements enter the models, so those judgements are only part of the story.

I will close with two points. In this Australian survey, stronger vertical and harmony orientations are consistently associated with weaker support for liberal democracy. External efficacy and credulous trust also have negative associations under both performance criteria, while the internal-efficacy and cynical-mistrust expectations receive weaker or no clear support. The broader implication is that confidence in government tells us less about democratic commitment than we might assume unless we ask what citizens think government has done. Our evidence is cross-sectional, and the four-category equations were fitted separately, so the theoretical arrows remain propositions for further study. The appendix contains the exact item coding, model denominators and sensitivity checks. Thank you; I welcome your questions.

These are backup slides for questions about measurement and model choice. I would not present them in the timed talk unless there is a particular question from the audience. The first slides set out the exact items and coding; the later slides give the analytical denominators and the main sensitivity findings.

These are the principal works behind the outcome measure, the trust typology, the cultural-orientation argument and the efficacy items. The manuscript and its online appendix contain the full reference list and the operational details.

The cultural scales each average two responses. Vertical orientation combines deference to parents and teachers, while harmony combines concern about group division and divergent ways of thinking. These are focused measures, not full accounts of either cultural tradition. The efficacy items distinguish confidence in one's own political understanding from beliefs about whether politicians are responsive. The efficacy pairs have stronger internal consistency than the cultural pairs, especially harmony. That is one reason we interpret the cultural coefficients as associations with these measured beliefs rather than with a broad cultural syndrome.

The threshold is worth spelling out. Trust and strong trust form the trusting category. The midpoint is grouped with distrust responses as non-trust; it does not mean that every person in this category actively distrusts government. A big or very big problem counts as severe. Other substantive responses count as not severe, and don't-know answers are missing. We pair federal-government trust separately with corruption and service delivery. Because the problem questions refer to Australia broadly, the resulting labels are approximations of Norris's categories based on subjective assessments.

The different sample sizes arise because each model block requires a different set of non-missing answers. Efficacy equations have the broadest coverage; the latent support equations require the support items as well as the cultural, efficacy, trust and control variables. All equations use the survey weights and the same demographic and political-interest controls. The online appendix reports the complete fitted models. Since the four trust categories enter separately estimated multinomial and support equations, we do not calculate a formal indirect effect through that typology.

The sensitivity analysis has two messages. The credulous-trust contrast remains similar when the harmony scale gains a third item. It changes more when we use explicit distrust as the threshold, particularly for service delivery. The court-based classification also gives a different pattern from the federal-government classification, so the trust object is substantively important. A binary mismatch indicator produces a negative association with support, but it merges the credulous and cynical cases that the main analysis distinguishes. In the joint binary model, the defined indirect-path intervals include zero; that check does not justify a mediation claim for the four-type analysis.
